assessment.Expression at the core of Article 10: The applicant took part in a political demonstration concerning the opening of the ECB headquarters and wore a transparent visor bearing the slogan "smash capitalism" (see paragraphs 5 and 6). That conduct was not purely functional: it conveyed an anti-capitalist political message in the context of a public protest. Political expression in a demonstration setting attracts a high level of protection under Article 10, especially where the message concerns matters of public interest (see nos. 8080/08, 29580/12, 32152/04).

assessment.Existence of an interference: The applicant was subjected to criminal proceedings and ultimately convicted and fined for wearing the visor during the demonstration (see paragraphs 8-15). A criminal conviction, even where the final penalty is relatively low, is a clear interference with freedom of expression and is capable of producing a chilling effect on participation in future protests (see nos. 68514/01, 25196/04, 37553/05).

assessment.Prescribed by law and foreseeability: The interference had a formal basis in sections 17a and 27 of the Act on Public Assemblies and Processions (see paragraphs 17 and 18). However, the foreseeability of the applicant's conviction is doubtful. The legislative materials define "protective weapons" as objects normally manufactured for defence, such as protective shields, armour, steel helmets or gas masks, and they expressly indicate that symbolic use solely for the expression of opinion is not covered (see paragraph 19). The applicant's object was a simple piece of transparent plastic sheeting, with a political inscription added by him, and the police on the spot neither warned him, fined him, nor asked him to remove it (see paragraph 6). The domestic courts' reasoning appears strained, particularly the Regional Court's statement that the object's protective purpose had been assigned "at the time of manufacture" because of the inscription "smash capitalism" (see paragraph 13). In these circumstances, it is questionable whether the applicant could reasonably have foreseen that his makeshift visor would be treated as a criminally prohibited protective weapon (see nos. 20652/92, 37101/97, 15367/14).

assessment.Legitimate aim: The impugned measure pursued legitimate aims under Article 10 § 2, namely the prevention of disorder or crime and the protection of public safety. The background to the demonstration was exceptionally tense: in the same area and during the same time frame, violent groups erected barricades, set fires, damaged cars, attacked police and emergency services, and injured officers (see paragraph 7). The State was therefore entitled to take precautions against escalation and against equipment intended to neutralise police measures (see nos. 8029/07, 7871/10).

assessment.Assessment of necessity: relevance of th: The violent context is an important factor, but it cannot by itself justify criminally sanctioning every unusual form of protest expression. The applicant participated in a demonstration advertised as "colourful, loud – but peaceful" and there is no finding that he himself committed or incited violence, concealed his identity, resisted police, or was linked to the violent groups active nearby (see paragraphs 6 and 7). The Court's case-law requires an individualised assessment; a peaceful protester should not be penalised merely because disorder occurred elsewhere in the same protest environment (see nos. 50841/99, 23086/08, 74768/10).

assessment.Assessment of necessity: sufficiency of: The domestic courts relied essentially on the abstract view that the visor could help protect the eyes from pepper spray and thus prolong the applicant's ability to resist police measures (see paragraphs 10 and 13). Yet they did not identify any concrete conduct by the applicant showing readiness for violence. They also gave insufficient weight to the expressive element of the visor. Their response that the applicant could have worn the visor on the back of his head if he merely wished to display the slogan (see paragraph 11) did not properly address his freedom to choose the manner of expressing his message. Moreover, section 17a(4) itself envisaged less restrictive on-site responses, such as orders or exclusion from the event (see paragraph 17), but the police took no such steps during the demonstration (see paragraph 6). Resorting afterwards to a criminal conviction therefore appears disproportionate. Even though the final fine was reduced to ten daily rates (see paragraph 12), the criminal nature of the sanction remained capable of discouraging political expression at demonstrations (see nos. 30582/04, 31684/05, 68537/13).

assessment.Overall conclusion: Balancing the applicant's strong interest in political expression against the authorities' interest in preventing disorder, the domestic courts appear to have given decisive weight to an expansive and arguably unforeseeable interpretation of "protective weapon" and to an abstract risk assessment, without demonstrating a concrete and pressing social need to impose a criminal penalty on this applicant. In light of the heightened protection afforded to political protest, the reasons relied on were not sufficient to show that the interference was necessary in a democratic society (see nos. 17526/10, 26986/03, 8577/08).
